title: Chinese Lamb with Cumin
subtitle: Xinjiang-style cumin lamb stir-fried with dried chilli and spring onion
excerpt: This Xinjiang street-food classic coats thin-sliced lamb in toasted cumin, dried chilli, and soy, then stir-fries over high heat until fragrant and slightly charred at the edges. Ready in 20 minutes once the lamb is sliced. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Xinjiang cumin lamb (zi ran yang rou) originates in the cuisine of Xinjiang province in northwest China, where the Uyghur, Kazakh, and Han populations share a tradition of lamb cooked with cumin, dried chilli, and Sichuan peppercorn. The dish reflects the region's position on ancient Silk Road trading routes and appears in Fuchsia Dunlop's Land of Plenty as a northern Chinese street staple. It has become one of the most recognisable dishes of Chinese northwest cuisine in restaurants globally.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the lamb up to 4 hours ahead, covered in the fridge.

content.text: Xinjiang cumin lamb is ready in 20 minutes and serves four. The lamb is sliced thin, velveted, and stir-fried at high heat with whole cumin seeds, dried chillies, and garlic. The cumin goes in twice: early to bloom in oil, and again at the end for raw fragrance.

Slice the lamb as thinly as possible -- 3-4 mm -- across the grain. Partially freezing the lamb for 20 minutes makes this much easier. A hot, dry wok with very little oil is the other requirement: too much oil and the lamb steams instead of searing, losing the char that defines the dish.

content.text: In a bowl, combine the sliced lamb with 10 ml of the light soy sauce, the
, and half the cracked cumin. Toss well and leave to marinate for 10 minutes.

Heat the wok over the highest possible flame until it smokes. Add the vegetable oil and swirl, then let any oil that coats the sides burn off for 10 seconds. The wok should be extremely hot before the lamb goes in.
Spread the lamb in a single layer in the wok and leave undisturbed for 45 seconds -- the
and heat will begin to char the edges. Toss vigorously and stir-fry for a further 2 minutes.
Push the lamb to one side of the wok. Add the garlic, ginger, and dried chillies to the cleared space and stir-fry for 30 seconds until the garlic starts to colour. Toss everything together.

Add the remaining light soy, the crushed Sichuan peppercorns, and the remaining cracked cumin. Toss to coat the lamb, then add the spring onion lengths. Stir-fry for 1 minute more until the spring onion is wilted but still has some bite.
Season with salt, drizzle with sesame oil, and toss once more. Transfer to a serving plate and serve immediately with flatbread or steamed rice.

items.symptom: Lamb is grey and steamed rather than charred
items.cause: Too much oil, wok not hot enough, or lamb was crowded
items.fix: Cook in two batches if needed. The wok must be smoking before the lamb goes in. Use minimal oil.

items.cause: Cumin was not toasted before going into the wok, or added too late
items.fix: Toast the cumin seeds dry in a pan for 60 seconds before cracking. Add half to the marinade so it blooms in the oil when the lamb hits the wok.

items.cause: Dried chillies or cumin were scorched rather than toasted
items.fix: Reduce heat slightly if the chillies turn black rather than deep red. A brief char on the lamb is desirable; blackened spices are not.

content.text: This dish comes from Xinjiang in northwest China, a region with Central Asian and Muslim culinary traditions. Lamb and cumin are central to Uyghur cooking. The stir-fried version is popular at Xinjiang restaurants across China. It goes well with flatbread or rice.
